questions.prompt: A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if and only if:

options.text: R1 ∩ R2 is a superkey of R1 or of R2
Both R1 and R2 are in BCNF

questions.explanation: The common attributes must functionally determine all of at least one fragment. A non-empty intersection alone is insufficient — without the FD, the natural join produces spurious tuples.

questions.prompt: Which statement about BCNF decomposition is TRUE?

options.text: BCNF decomposition is always dependency preserving but may be lossy
Every BCNF decomposition preserves all functional dependencies
A lossless BCNF decomposition always exists, but it may not preserve all dependencies
Some relations admit no lossless BCNF decomposition

questions.explanation: A lossless join into BCNF is always achievable, but dependency preservation can be impossible — the classic example is R(A,B,C) with AB → C and C → B. 3NF, by contrast, guarantees both.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C, D) with FDs {A → B, B → CD}. Is this decomposition lossless?

options.text: Yes — but only because A → B holds
No — B determines nothing in either fragment
Yes — B is a key of R2

questions.explanation: The intersection is {B}, and B → CD makes B a superkey of R2(B,C,D). That satisfies the lossless-join condition, so the natural join reconstructs R exactly.

questions.prompt: A relation R is in 4NF if, for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X ↠ Y:

options.text: X is a superkey of R
Y is a superkey of R

questions.explanation: 4NF extends BCNF from functional to multivalued dependencies: every non-trivial MVD must have a superkey determinant. This removes the redundancy caused by two independent multivalued facts sharing a relation.

questions.prompt: Which normal form addresses join dependencies that are not implied by candidate keys?
questions.explanation: 5NF concerns relations that cannot be losslessly decomposed into two fragments but can be into three or more. 4NF handles multivalued dependencies, a special case of join dependencies.

questions.prompt: A decomposition of R into R1, ..., Rn preserves dependencies if:

options.text: Every FD in F appears within a single Ri
The union of the FDs projected onto each Ri has the same closure as F

questions.explanation: What matters is closure equivalence, not literal containment: an FD may be enforceable indirectly from the projected dependencies even if it spans two fragments.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C) has FDs {A → B, B → C}. Decomposing into R1(A, B) and R2(A, C) — what is the outcome?
questions.explanation: The intersection {A} is a superkey of both fragments, so the join is lossless. But B → C spans the split: R1 yields A → B and R2 yields A → C, and their closure cannot derive B → C. So it is lost.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a trivial multivalued dependency on R(A, B)?

options.text: A ↠ B where B is a superkey
A ↠ B where A ∪ B = R
No MVD on two attributes can be trivial
A ↠ B where A is a foreign key

questions.explanation: An MVD X ↠ Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X or when X ∪ Y is the whole relation. Trivial MVDs impose no constraint and so never violate 4NF.

questions.prompt: Why is 3NF sometimes preferred over BCNF in practical schema design?

options.text: 3NF guarantees a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition; BCNF does not
3NF requires fewer relations in every case

questions.explanation: There is always a 3NF decomposition that is both lossless and dependency preserving. Forcing BCNF may cost dependency preservation, meaning constraints must be checked by joining at runtime.

questions.prompt: For F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}, which is a valid canonical cover?
questions.explanation: A → C is implied by A → B and B → C, so it is extraneous; AB → C has the extraneous attribute B. What remains is {A → B, B → C}, whose closure equals F's with no redundant FD or attribute.
